messages.author: f08a70118f19e2a0
messages.subject: Vectorized Nodes with Data Augmentation?
parts:
Hi everyone,

First, I want to say that I just participated in the remote NIMBLE workshop, and I thought it was really great. It has really helped me think about the problem that I'm working on, and now I have a question that I'm hoping for some help with. I'm going to try to post a version of the code without all the gory details, but I'm happy to share more if that helps.

I'm trying to model habitat selection of elk from many years of aerial surveys, but with imperfect detection. The complication arises because elk form groups of widely varying sizes (a handful of individuals up to >1000 individuals). Assuming that detection is equal no matter the group size is therefore unreasonable. I have the sizes of the observed groups, and I've turned to data augmentation to assign a group size to the unobserved groups.

I'm quite happy with the conceptual model structure I've developed, but the problem is that it is basically impossible to fit as I've written it. I've got three for() loops to index across time, spatial cell, and group (with augmentation), and I wind up with a model that has hundreds of thousands of scalar nodes. My computer with 64 GB of RAM crashes just trying to configure the MCMC. For a small subset of spatial cells (100 out of ~ 2500), if I set useConjugacy = FALSE in configureMCMC, I am able to at least configure and run the MCMC, and the results are sensible (after a few days), but I don't think I can scale this up for my full analysis.

After the workshop, I've been thinking about vectorizing (matrix-izing?) my calculations across space and groups, especially since once the habitat selection parameters are updated, all the space and group calculations need to be redone anyway. I wrote some custom distributions that return a logProb from a matrix, and I got my model all the way down to ~300 multivariate nodes (still looping over time, but not space or group). I built the whole model and got the MCMC running super fast, but when I got my samples back, I discovered that I had exactly my priors/inits... and then I realized that because I had NAs in my multivariate nodes, they were not being treated as data, and the rDIST was overwriting my data values. Here is a reduced version of the model code as it stands:


elkCode <- nimbleCode({
 
  ########## Priors ##########
 
  mu_N_t1 ~ dnorm(prior_N_t1, sd = 1000)
 
  #Annual growth rate (lambda)
  mu_lambda ~ dnorm(1, sd = 1000)
  tau_lambda ~ dgamma(0.01, 0.01)
 
  #alpha (covariates for HS)
  for (i in 1:3){
    alpha[i] ~ dnorm(0, sd = 1)
  }
 
  #beta (covariates for lambda)
  #for (i in 1:3){
  #  beta[i] ~ dnorm(0, 1.0E-3)
  #}
 
  #gamma (covariates for N_p)
  #Informed prior from previous analysis
  gamma[1] ~ dnorm(gamma_b0_mu, tau = gamma_b0_tau)
  gamma[2] ~ dnorm(gamma_b1_mu, tau = gamma_b1_tau)
 
  #delta (covariates for p)
  #Informed prior from previous analysis
  delta[1] ~ dnorm(delta_b0_mu, tau = delta_b0_tau)
  delta[2] ~ dnorm(delta_b1_mu, tau = delta_b1_tau)
  delta[3] ~ dnorm(delta_b2_mu, tau = delta_b2_tau)
 
  ########## Likelihood ##########
 
  #### ... Fully vectorized ####
  #Average group size experienced by an individual (parameter of the group distribution)
  log(N_p[1:Omega, 1:length_t]) <- gamma[1] + gamma[2] * open[1:Omega, 1:length_t]
 
  #### ... Time dependent ####
 
  #### ... ... Unique t == 1 ####
  for (t in 1:1){
    #Expected population in the first year
    E_N[t] <- mu_N_t1
  }
 
  #### ... ... Unique t > 1 ####
  for (t in 2:length_t){
    #Draw lambda
    lambda[t] ~ T(dnorm(mu_lambda, tau_lambda), 0, 2)
   
    #Expected population that year
    E_N[t] <- N[t - 1] * lambda[t]
  }
 
  #### ... ... All times ####
  for (t in 1:length_t){
   
    #Habitat selection
    HS[1:Omega, t] <- exp(alpha[1] * rough[1:Omega] +
                            alpha[2] * elev[1:Omega] +
                            #Openness is time-varying
                            alpha[3] * open[1:Omega, t])

    #Group sizes (custom distribution that includes 0 in its support)
    N_itg[1:Omega, t, 1:M] ~ dGroups(Omega = Omega,
                                     M = M,
                                     E_N = E_N[t],
                                     Np = N_p[1:Omega, t],
                                     HS = HS[1:Omega, t])
   
    #Zeroes are not real groups (binary matrix, "real" or not)
    z[1:Omega, t, 1:M] <- make_z(N_itg[1:Omega, t, 1:M]) #returns N_itg > 0
     
    #Group observation
    logit(p[1:Omega, t, 1:M]) <- delta[1] + delta[2] * open[1:Omega, t] + delta[3] * N_itg[1:Omega, t, 1:M]
    obs_prob[1:Omega, t, 1:M] <- p[1:Omega, t, 1:M] * z[1:Omega, t, 1:M] #can't be observed if it isn't real

    #Bernoulli Matrix (observed or not?)
    y[1:Omega, t, 1:M] ~ dBern_mat(prob = obs_prob[1:Omega, t, 1:M], Omega = Omega, M = M)
   
    #True population size
    N[t] <- sum(N_itg[1:Omega, t, 1:M])
  }
})



Note that `N_itg`, `z`, and `y` are passed as data. Only `y` (observed/unobserved) has no NAs. `N_itg` contains group size for observed groups and NAs for the augmented groups. `z = 1` for the observed groups and `z = NA` for the augmented groups.

Okay, so finally, here's my question. How can I take advantage of the efficiency of the multivariate node specification without hitting this issue? I have seen in other posts (and section 6.1.1.3 of the NIMBLE User Manual) that multivariate nodes must be entirely observed or not observed at all, but also a hint from Perry that it might be possible to build a work-around. One thought I had was that maybe I could try to write the rDIST so that you pass it the index of the data as an argument so that it does not overwrite it. Would this possibly work? Any other thoughts?

The other idea that was mentioned in the workshop was using sparse-data representations. Any pointers to resources for that?

Thanks a bunch for your time and help.

Brian Smith

messages.author: 5fa2a363d4ddd1d1
messages.subject: Re: Vectorized Nodes with Data Augmentation?
parts:
Hi Brian, some thoughts here (though there is a bit I am not following):

1) In the MCMC, you need to sample the group size of the unobserved groups and keep the size of the observed groups fixed.

To do this, I would set N_itg via 'inits'. Then remove any samplers assigned by default to N_itg  and instead assign individual samplers only to the elements of N_itg that are NA. Given N_itg is discrete, one option is the categorical sampler (unless the group size is unbounded) but this may be slow given the group size could be any of many discrete values. So using the slice sampler may be better.

That should ensure that the known values of N_itg stay at their actual values during MCMC. This essentially tricks the MCMC into treating those elements
as 'data' though they are not flagged as 'data' in the model. 

2) It's not clear to me why 'z' for an augmented group is NA rather than 0.  Could 'z' just be set as an array of 0s and 1s via 'constants'?
2a) Isn't there a non-zero probability of observing the augmented (unobserved) groups, it just happens that they weren't observed?
2b) I'm almost certainly missing something but it's not clear to me why you need 'z' at all. 

3) For clarification, 'rDIST' is not involved here. Rather the non-NA values are being overwritten because they are assigned an MCMC sampler. So it is the sampler that is overwriting them, not any sort of drawing values from their prior.

-chris

messages.author: dd632bd3bbcdd7e9
messages.subject: Re: Vectorized Nodes with Data Augmentation?
parts:
Let me add some thoughts on this as well.

For a variable that is a mix of observed and unobserved, I think the following works well:
provide it in data with values for observed elements and NAs for unobserved elements, and also
provide it in inits with NAs for the observed elements and values for unobserved elements.

It's hard to follow more closely without more explanation of the notation and the intent of different parts of the model.  It may be that it would make sense to vectorize in 1:Omega or 1:M but not both.

We do not have a default way to sample only unobserved elements of a multivariate node, or (I think) an arbitrary discrete multivariate node.  Chris' suggestion of assigning a scalar sampler to those elements manually makes sense.

I am guessing you are thinking of z in its common use in data augmentation in ecological models as an indicator or whether a virtual individual is "real" as an implementation of a flat prior on number of never-observed individuals (or groups in your case).  However, you have z as a deterministic node, so it doesn't make sense to have z be data.  Only stochastic nodes should be data.

A little more on the ecology side, you are probably well aware of this, but I note that often environmental stochasticity in population change is set up as normally distributed on a log scale, whereas you have it as normal on the population scale (E_N[t] <- N[t - 1] * lambda[t]) if I follow.  Nevermind if that's not the point.

Beyond this, if you are still stuck please provide a minimal reproducible example.

-Perry

messages.subject: Re: Vectorized Nodes with Data Augmentation?
parts:
Hi Chris and Perry,

Thank you both for your replies. Your suggestions were really helpful, and I was able to specify which nodes of N_itg to sample during the MCMC. At least in a preliminary run, the MCMC was successfully updating values. I'll have to wait for a longer run to confirm that the results are sensible.

Just a few follow-ups: 

Yes, I'm using z the way you guess, Perry. My "proposed groups" can fall into 3 categories: (1) real and observed, z = 1, y = 1; (2) real, but not observed, z = 1, y = 0; or (3) not real (thus unobservable), z = 0, y = 0. It does seem kind of silly since my z's are actually deterministic nodes under my current formulation, but I can estimate Pr(z = 1) from some expectations, given habitat selection and total abundance, so I can estimate the likelihood along with the group sizes. I left all the details out, but that's part of what's happening in dGroups(). I think I still need z, though, because detection is conditional on z == 1: (obs_prob[1:Omega, t, 1:M] <- p[1:Omega, t, 1:M] * z[1:Omega, t, 1:M] #can't be observed if it isn't real). I'm definitely open to suggestions on how to improve that, but it seems to be working this way.

Also, good catch on the population change, Perry. I actually had that as just sort of a place holder, which I've switched to a Ricker model, but I did wind up specifying it on the log scale.

On Thursday, June 11, 2020 at 11:36:00 AM UTC-6, pdevalpine wrote:

Let me add some thoughts on this as well.

For a variable that is a mix of observed and unobserved, I think the following works well:
provide it in data with values for observed elements and NAs for unobserved elements, and also
provide it in inits with NAs for the observed elements and values for unobserved elements.

It's hard to follow more closely without more explanation of the notation and the intent of different parts of the model.  It may be that it would make sense to vectorize in 1:Omega or 1:M but not both.

We do not have a default way to sample only unobserved elements of a multivariate node, or (I think) an arbitrary discrete multivariate node.  Chris' suggestion of assigning a scalar sampler to those elements manually makes sense.

I am guessing you are thinking of z in its common use in data augmentation in ecological models as an indicator or whether a virtual individual is "real" as an implementation of a flat prior on number of never-observed individuals (or groups in your case).  However, you have z as a deterministic node, so it doesn't make sense to have z be data.  Only stochastic nodes should be data.

A little more on the ecology side, you are probably well aware of this, but I note that often environmental stochasticity in population change is set up as normally distributed on a log scale, whereas you have it as normal on the population scale (E_N[t] <- N[t - 1] * lambda[t]) if I follow.  Nevermind if that's not the point.

Beyond this, if you are still stuck please provide a minimal reproducible example.

-Perry
On Wed, Jun 10, 2020 at 11:45 AM Chris Paciorek <christoph...@gmail.com> wrote:

Hi Brian, some thoughts here (though there is a bit I am not following):

1) In the MCMC, you need to sample the group size of the unobserved groups and keep the size of the observed groups fixed.

To do this, I would set N_itg via 'inits'. Then remove any samplers assigned by default to N_itg  and instead assign individual samplers only to the elements of N_itg that are NA. Given N_itg is discrete, one option is the categorical sampler (unless the group size is unbounded) but this may be slow given the group size could be any of many discrete values. So using the slice sampler may be better.

That should ensure that the known values of N_itg stay at their actual values during MCMC. This essentially tricks the MCMC into treating those elements
as 'data' though they are not flagged as 'data' in the model. 

2) It's not clear to me why 'z' for an augmented group is NA rather than 0.  Could 'z' just be set as an array of 0s and 1s via 'constants'?
2a) Isn't there a non-zero probability of observing the augmented (unobserved) groups, it just happens that they weren't observed?
2b) I'm almost certainly missing something but it's not clear to me why you need 'z' at all. 

3) For clarification, 'rDIST' is not involved here. Rather the non-NA values are being overwritten because they are assigned an MCMC sampler. So it is the sampler that is overwriting them, not any sort of drawing values from their prior.

-chris
